title: Weaponized Institutional Knowledge
intro: Institutional knowledge is valuable — until it's used to shut down research. "Our users are different" is the most dangerous phrase in UX because it replaces evidence with tenure.

learn.title: The 90/10 rule
learn.text:
NNG analyzed its own foundational usability guidelines and found they produce a usable design about **90% of the time**.

That leaves roughly 10% of cases where breaking a best practice might produce something better.

So why do teams break best practices by default? The burden of proof belongs on the person who wants to deviate — and they need **behavioral data**, not anecdotes or seniority.

try.q: A stakeholder says "Our power users don't need icon labels." Who should provide evidence?
options: The stakeholder — they're claiming an exception to a best practice
The designer — they need to prove labels work
Nobody — it's a matter of preference
The engineering team — they decide what ships
try.explain: The burden of proof is on whoever claims their case is the exception. Best practices are the default.

learn.title: "Our users are different"
learn.text:
The most common claims that shut down research:

→ "Users have memorized our icon language, labels would clutter the UI"
→ "Technical users like jargon and dense layouts"
→ "Users don't scroll, everything must be above the fold"
→ "No accessibility needs — nobody's complained"

Across ~20 years and several companies, the author tested icon-only navigation in **seven organizations**. Each time, participants — including power users — struggled. Almost every "our users are different" claim, when tested, matched standard best practices.

left.label: What they say
items: We've always done it this way

try.q: A PM says: "No one has complained about accessibility, so we're fine." What's wrong with this logic?
options: Absence of complaints doesn't mean absence of problems
try.explain: Users who can't use a product often leave quietly. No complaints ≠ no problems.

learn.title: Six ways institutional knowledge hurts UX
learn.text:
1. **Shuts down research before it starts** — "We already know our users"
2. **Flips the burden of proof** — researchers must disprove claims instead of claimants validating them
3. **Introduces bias in research** — SME-mindset interviewers lead users and steer answers
4. **Limits participant pool** — the same "champion" users become unofficial team members
5. **Turns research into a formality** — polished presentations to focus groups seek confirmation
6. **Creates subtle validation bias** — researchers over-identify with users and miss blind spots

The fix: start with best practices. Exceptions need behavioral evidence. If no one is ever confused in your sessions, your research may be flawed.

try.q: Your team always tests with the same 5 "champion" users who know the product well. What's the risk?
options: You'll miss confusion that new users experience
try.explain: Champion users are too familiar with the product. Rotate participants and seek new voices to find real usability problems.

test.q: According to the 90/10 rule, what percentage of the time do established usability best practices produce a usable design?
test.explain: NNG's analysis found best practices work about 90% of the time. The 10% exception requires behavioral evidence.

test.q: When someone says "our users are different" to argue against a best practice, who holds the burden of proof?
test.explain: The burden of proof is on whoever wants to break from a best practice. They need behavioral data, not opinions.

test.q: Icon-only navigation was tested across seven organizations. What was the consistent finding?
options: Even power users struggled without labels
test.explain: In every test, participants — including power users — struggled with icon-only navigation. Labels consistently help.

options: When it replaces user data to stop research or win arguments
When it's used by senior employees
test.explain: Institutional knowledge becomes weaponized when it's used to end conversations, block research, or override evidence with seniority.

test.q: If no participant is ever confused during your research sessions, what should you suspect?
options: The research methodology may be flawed
Your sample size is too small
test.explain: Some confusion is normal. If nobody struggles, you may be testing with too-familiar users or leading them through the tasks.
